newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU oilseed markets brace for US gene-soy arrivals.
newsitem.headline: EU oilseed markets brace for US gene-soy arrivals.

text.p: A row over the use of genetically modified soybeans in Europe may come to a head with the first shipment of 1996 crop U.S. beans due in Germany early next week.
The first known U.S. new crop shipment, arriving shortly, may contain the new products as part of its 65,000-tonne cargo.
"We asked suppliers to separate new and traditional soybeans but we were unsuccessful," said Arnd von Wissel, chief of oil processing company Oelmuehle Hamburg AG.
"Meantime there is no alternative to using U.S. beans for the EU (animal) feeds and oils markets in the winter months."

Oilseeds markets were nervously watching market impact from lobby group furor over alleged health and environmentalist risks from the new products. The row has brought limited price support for domestic rapeseed oil.
"The consumer opposition seems centred in German speaking countries...perhaps markets will be able to find a localised solution," one oilseeds and products broker in Hamburg said.
Environmentalist group Greenpeace, which is campaigning against the new products, said it would make its voice heard.
"We want (processors) to state what they are crushing, where it goes and whether they plan to declare...gene-modified beans," said Joerg Naumann, Greenpeace campaign leader in Hamburg.
Von Wissel, who pointed out the new products had been found safe by health authorities in all countries concerned, said his company was ready to await and assess possible protests.
Dutch activists said ahead of arrivals in that country they could "never rule out direct action in our campaigns."
Greenpeace activities have resulted in a number of large German food companies promising to keep products derived from the new beans out of their product range.
Some 60 percent of all foodstuffs contain soya products.
Developed by Monsanto Corp, the beans are resistant to a weedkiller, which saves farmers input costs, but opponents say too little is known about side-effects.

With European food companies looking to replace U.S. soya with dwindling Latin American beans or domestic rapeseed, EU rapeseed oil has an atypical premium over soy oil. But this is also a result of rapeseed shortages.
Processing sources said they could also crush tropical seeds and sunflowerseed to get around the soybean problems.
"And if worst comes to worst, we could sell soy oil outside Germany, where we would concentrate rape oil sales," one said.

While Nestle and Unilever in Germany have said they will avoid the new products, their counterparts in other countries have been less prepared to do so. Nestle France said it would use them and Danone said it would use different strategies in France and Germany.

French Eridania Beghin Say and Lesieur and Italian Giglio Oro are ready to make oil from the new beans. Only Dutch Nutricia joined German firms saying its infant milk would not be made from genetically-modified beans.
Apart from the threat of consumer boycotts, activists are also pressing EU legislators to agree labelling rules on so-called novel foods.
